statement: What is the sum of the squares of all real numbers $x$ that satisfy $x^2 - 12\lfloor x \rfloor + 20 = 0$? (Here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$.)

choices.misconception: I used strict inequalities on both ends, $n < x < n + 1$, which threw out the integer solutions $x = 2$ and $x = 10$.
I solved $n^2 \le 12n - 20$ as $2 \le n < 10$, dropping the endpoint $n = 10$, so I missed the solution $x = 10$.
I solved $n^2 \le 12n - 20$ as $2 < n \le 10$, dropping the endpoint $n = 2$, so I missed the solution $x = 2$.
I solved $12n - 20 \le (n + 1)^2$ with a non-strict inequality, so I wrongly kept $n = 3$ and $n = 7$, where $x = 4$ and $x = 8$ have the wrong floor.

hints: Then $x^2 = 12n - 20$, so $x = \pm\sqrt{12n - 20}$. Now demand that this $x$ really has floor $n$: $n \le x < n + 1$.
Negative $x$ is impossible because $12n - 20 \ge 0$ forces $n \ge 2$. For $x = \sqrt{12n - 20}$: $n^2 \le 12n - 20$ gives $2 \le n \le 10$, and $12n - 20 < (n + 1)^2$ gives $n < 3$ or $n > 7$.

solutions.reliable: Let $n = \lfloor x \rfloor$. Then $x^2 = 12n - 20$, so $12n - 20 \ge 0$ and $n \ge 2$, which makes $x \ge 2$ positive; thus $x = \sqrt{12n - 20}$. We need $n \le \sqrt{12n - 20} < n + 1$. The left part is $n^2 - 12n + 20 \le 0$, that is $(n - 2)(n - 10) \le 0$, so $2 \le n \le 10$. The right part is $12n - 20 < n^2 + 2n + 1$, that is $(n - 3)(n - 7) > 0$, so $n < 3$ or $n > 7$. Hence $n \in \{2, 8, 9, 10\}$, giving $x = 2, \sqrt{76}, \sqrt{88}, 10$. Check $n = 8$: $\sqrt{76} \approx 8.72$ has floor $8$; and $n = 7$ fails because $\sqrt{64} = 8$ has floor $8$, not $7$. The sum of squares is $\sum (12n - 20) = 4 + 76 + 88 + 100 = 268$. Transferable idea: with a floor, name the integer part, solve, then insist the answer actually has that integer part.
